Name: Adopt serverless architecture for AI/ML workload processes
Guideline: Building an ML model takes significant computing resources that need to be optimized for efficient utilization; using serverless architecture for AI/ML workload processes helps match resource consumption to actual demand.
Context: The pattern extends this across the whole ML lifecycle — data pipelines, training, experimentation — and flags a concrete tradeoff to check first: whether your workload can tolerate cold-start latency during initialization, since that's what serverless costs you in exchange for not paying for idle compute.

Name: Choose the region that is closest to users
Guideline: From an energy-efficiency perspective, it is better to shorten the distance a network packet travels so that less energy is required to transmit it, so choose the cloud region closest to your users.
Context: The pattern's practical test: pick the region serving the majority of where your traffic actually originates, not the region with the most features or the most popular choice — accepting that the closer region may lack some capabilities is the tradeoff this pattern asks you to make deliberately.

Name: Containerize your workloads
Guideline: Containerizing workloads enables better resource utilisation and bin packing, reducing unnecessary compute allocation and embodied carbon.
Context: The pattern's concrete tools are Docker and Kubernetes manifests, and it notes containerization alone may not be enough for a large monolithic application — pairing it with a microservice architecture is what actually enables independently right-sizing each component.

Name: Implement stateless design
Guideline: Applications that consume large memory or on-disk data require larger VM sizes, especially for cloud computing, so designing components to be stateless allows them to be right-sized and scaled more efficiently.
Context: The pattern points at a concrete methodology and mechanism: follow the 12-factor app methodology, and externalize state to a NoSQL database or in-memory cache service rather than holding it in the application instance itself.

Name: Queue non-urgent processing requests
Guideline: From a hardware-efficiency perspective, systems are more efficient when the impact of request spikes is minimised through even utilization, so non-urgent requests should be queued rather than processed immediately.
Context: The pattern's mechanism is a message queue decoupling components asynchronously, and it's explicit about the tradeoff: the added complexity of managing a queue has to be weighed against how much it actually helps your specific sustainability goals, not applied automatically everywhere.

Name: Run AI models at the edge
Guideline: Deploy AI inference on edge devices or local infrastructure to reduce data transfer, network energy use, and reliance on centralised cloud compute.
Context: The pattern names concrete tooling — TensorFlow Lite, ONNX Runtime, NVIDIA Jetson — and is upfront about the tradeoff: less network/cloud usage comes at the cost of more device management complexity and embodied emissions from the distributed hardware itself.

Name: Scale logical components independently
Guideline: Decomposing applications into independently scalable microservices allows each component to be right-sized for its own demand, avoiding over-provisioning of the whole system.
Context: The pattern adds a caution the base guideline doesn't: avoid creating overly granular microservices, and use a lightweight protocol like gRPC for inter-service communication, since the messaging/framework overhead between too many small services can eat into the efficiency gains.

Name: Select efficient accelerators and instance types for AI workloads
Guideline: Match AI workloads to the most energy-efficient hardware accelerator or instance type available to improve utilisation and reduce energy consumption.
Context: The pattern's process: profile workloads by latency, throughput, and execution characteristics before choosing hardware, then use orchestration to automatically route to the most energy-efficient available platform, tracked via continuous performance-per-watt benchmarking rather than a one-time hardware choice.

Name: Use on-demand execution for AI and agent workloads
Guideline: Trigger AI and agent workloads only when needed using serverless or event-driven platforms to eliminate idle compute.
Context: The pattern names the concrete platforms — AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, Azure Functions — and adds a specific agent-design requirement: workflows should terminate after task completion rather than staying resident, so an agent isn't left idly consuming resources between triggers.

Name: Evaluate other CPU architectures
Guideline: Applications are built with a software architecture that best fits the business need they are serving; evaluating alternative CPU architectures (e.g. ARM) can improve energy efficiency for a given workload.
Context: The pattern ties this directly to the Software Carbon Intensity formula: switching CPU architecture is framed as a direct lever on the Energy term specifically, and it suggests also considering specialized accelerators some cloud providers offer as a further option beyond just x86-vs-ARM.

Name: Use serverless cloud services
Guideline: Serverless cloud services scale dynamically with demand and share infrastructure across many applications, improving overall utilization and reducing embodied carbon compared to dedicated infrastructure.
Context: The pattern's practical caveat: moving to serverless may require a substantial redesign of the application rather than a drop-in swap, and — as with other serverless patterns here — whether your workload can tolerate cold-start latency is the key thing to evaluate before committing to it.

Name: Prioritise system-first typography selection based on user needs
Guideline: Align typography and component choices with actual user needs, preferring system fonts and existing assets over custom downloads to reduce unnecessary data transfer and rendering overhead.
Context: The pattern's concrete example of the waste it's targeting: loading a full Unicode character set when a site only actually needs Latin characters is called out as a common, avoidable source of excess weight — its fix, if a custom font really is necessary, is WOFF2 compression plus subsetting to the characters actually used.

Name: Avoid an excessive DOM size
Guideline: The greater the number of nodes defined in HTML, the greater the time spent processing and rendering each element, so keeping the DOM size small reduces energy used during rendering.
Context: The pattern's concrete technique for large lists specifically: Angular's virtual scrolling component or React windowing libraries like react-window, so only the DOM nodes actually visible on screen get rendered rather than the entire list at once.

Name: Avoid chaining critical requests
Guideline: Most web experiences require a lot of work from the user's browser; the greater the length of request chains and the larger the download sizes, the more significant the impact on page load performance and the energy required to render a page.
Context: The pattern is careful to note this isn't an absolute rule: some critical request chains are genuinely necessary, so the target is avoiding them except where they're truly unavoidable, not eliminating every dependent request regardless of purpose.

Name: Avoid tracking unnecessary data
Guideline: User tracking, data collection and targeting in things like advertisements are responsible for significant energy use in many digital products and services, so only track data that is actually needed.
Context: The pattern frames this as an audit exercise: distinguish data that's genuinely critical to the product from discretionary collection like advertising or behavioral tracking, and its SCI framing is that cutting the latter reduces both the energy term and the emissions-intensity term of the carbon calculation at once.

Name: Cache static data
Guideline: From an energy-efficiency perspective, it is better to reduce network traffic by reading data locally through a cache rather than accessing it remotely over the network.
Context: The pattern adds a caveat worth knowing: the carbon-reduction benefit assumes an in-memory cache on your own local servers — if you instead rely on external cache infrastructure over the network, much of the packet-distance savings this pattern is built around gets diminished.

Name: Compress stored data
Guideline: Storing uncompressed data wastes bandwidth and increases storage capacity requirements; applying appropriate compression reduces both.
Context: The pattern's explicit tradeoff: compression isn't free, so weigh the storage savings against the energy cost of the compression and decompression process itself, and pick the specific compression tool suited to each use case rather than applying one default everywhere.

Name: Compress transmitted data
Guideline: From an energy-efficiency perspective, it is better to minimise the size of the data transmitted so that less energy is required because network traffic is reduced.
Context: The pattern flags the same tradeoff as compressing stored data: the compression/decompression cycle itself has a modest energy cost, so the net benefit depends on that overhead staying smaller than the network savings — which it usually does, with lower cloud transfer costs as a secondary benefit.

Name: Defer offscreen images
Guideline: Web pages often include images that are not displayed on the first loaded screen and can thus be loaded dynamically (lazy-loaded) instead of upfront, reducing unnecessary data transfer.
Context: The pattern's concrete implementation is the browser-native `loading="lazy"` HTML attribute (polyfillable for older browsers), and it specifically calls out content hidden behind tabs or accordions as a case that benefits as much as content simply below the fold.

Name: Deprecate GIFs for animated content
Guideline: A direct replacement for the GIF is the MP4 video format, which provides much smaller file sizes and higher quality at the same time, reducing bandwidth and storage use.
Context: The pattern also names alternatives beyond MP4 conversion: CSS animations, SVG animations, or modern image formats that support animation natively — with browser support being the main practical factor in choosing which replacement fits a given use case.

Name: Enable text compression
Guideline: Web browsers often communicate with web servers in human-readable formats such as HTML, JavaScript, CSS and JSON; compressing these text responses reduces the amount of data transmitted.
Context: The pattern's concrete mechanism: browsers and servers negotiate the compression format dynamically via the `Accept-Encoding`/`Content-Encoding` HTTP headers, so enabling this on the server side doesn't require picking one format upfront — the two ends agree on it automatically per request.

Name: Keep request counts low
Guideline: Accessing a web page usually retrieves an HTML file from the web server, which may then reference many additional resources the browser has to download; keeping the number of such requests low reduces network energy use.
Context: The pattern's concrete practice: set a request-count budget and measure it automatically as part of your test suite, so a creeping increase in the number of requests gets caught the same way a performance regression would, rather than discovered after the fact.

Name: Leverage pre-trained models and transfer learning
Guideline: Fine-tune existing pre-trained models instead of training from scratch to dramatically reduce the compute, energy, and time required for model development.
Context: The pattern's concrete resource is the Hugging Face Model Hub for finding domain-adapted or task-specific pre-trained models, alongside a caution worth weighing: a pre-trained model brings along its original training data's licensing terms and potential biases, not just its efficiency benefit.

Name: Minimize main thread work
Guideline: Long-running JavaScript on the browser's main thread underutilises multi-core CPUs; offloading heavy computations to Web Workers or server-side implementations reduces energy consumption.
Context: The pattern gives a rough concrete threshold: computations running longer than a few hundred milliseconds on the main thread are the ones worth moving — either to a Web Worker client-side, or to an optimized server-side implementation that can execute the same algorithm more efficiently than the browser can.

Name: Minimize the total number of deployed environments
Guideline: Each additional deployed environment has an increasing energy impact, which in turn creates more emissions, so it is important to understand the necessity of each environment and its environmental impact.
Context: The pattern's concrete practice: repurpose an existing environment for a second use — combining QA and performance testing environments, for example — rather than standing up a new one, while weighing the resulting workflow bottlenecks against the environmental and cost savings.

Name: Optimize agent orchestration to reduce unnecessary model calls
Guideline: Design agentic AI workflows to minimise redundant model invocations and unnecessary compute through caching, conditional logic, and efficient orchestration patterns.
Context: The pattern's concrete technique: use a smaller, cheaper model or plain heuristics to handle routing and filtering decisions before ever invoking a larger model, and use direct tool calls instead of a model transformation for simple data tasks — frameworks like LangChain, LlamaIndex, and AutoGen are named as supporting this kind of orchestration.

Name: Optimize data storage formats for AI training and inference
Guideline: Use efficient storage formats, compression, and indexing strategies for AI datasets and embeddings to reduce storage footprint, data transfer, and retrieval compute.
Context: The pattern's concrete formats: columnar storage like Parquet or ORC instead of text-based CSV for large datasets, and for vector embeddings specifically, indexing tools like FAISS, Milvus, or Pinecone rather than a naive linear scan.

Name: Optimize image size
Guideline: Ideally, stored pixel dimensions are exactly the same as, or smaller than, the display size in pixels so that no bandwidth or storage space is wasted on oversized images.
Context: The pattern's concrete implementation: generate multiple sized versions of each image — either through a CI/CD pipeline step or a third-party Image CDN service — so the browser can request the one closest to its actual display size, and consider SVG instead of a raster format entirely for images that need to scale dynamically.

Name: Reduce transmitted data
Guideline: From an energy-efficiency perspective, it is better to minimize the size of the data transmitted so that less energy is required because the network traffic is reduced.
Context: The pattern's concrete practice: send only the specific properties or values actually needed rather than a full object, and notes the data format itself matters a lot here — Protobuf, for instance, is notably more compact than XML for the same data — while flagging that omitted fields may add reconstruction overhead if they're needed again later.

Name: Remove unused CSS definitions
Guideline: CSS files are complex and require energy-intensive parsing and processing; each added CSS definition increases the amount of time and processing power needed, so unused rules should be removed.
Context: The pattern's concrete practice: consolidate multiple CSS files into one to cut processing overhead, with an explicit exception for landing pages with genuinely distinct layouts, where keeping a separate optimized stylesheet still makes sense rather than forcing everything into one shared file.

Name: Select efficient ML frameworks and inference runtimes
Guideline: Choose ML frameworks and inference runtimes that best match your hardware and workload to reduce compute overhead and improve energy efficiency.
Context: The pattern names concrete inference runtimes to evaluate — ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, OpenVINO — and stresses benchmarking them under your actual workload conditions rather than trusting published numbers, since ONNX as a portable format is specifically useful if you need the option to move between hardware environments later.

Name: Serve images in modern formats
Guideline: Modern image formats can help reduce bandwidth, storage and computing requirements on the displaying device compared to legacy formats.
Context: The pattern gives a concrete figure: WebP offers around 30% smaller file sizes than JPEG with no drop in quality, which is the kind of number worth citing when justifying the format switch — AVIF is the other modern format it suggests evaluating alongside WebP for compression/quality/compatibility tradeoffs.

Name: Terminate TLS at border gateway
Guideline: Transport Layer Security (TLS) ensures that data passed between web servers and browsers remains private and encrypted; however, repeatedly terminating and re-establishing TLS increases CPU usage, so terminating it at the border gateway can reduce overhead.
Context: The pattern's specific architecture: terminate TLS once at the border gateway, then continue non-TLS internally to the load balancer and workload — explicitly framed as a "Just Enough Security" tradeoff that doesn't apply if your application has a genuine end-to-end encryption compliance requirement.

Name: Use Asynchronous network calls instead of synchronous
Guideline: When making calls across process boundaries to databases, file systems or REST APIs, relying on synchronous calls can cause the calling thread to become blocked and waste resources; asynchronous calls avoid this.
Context: The pattern ties this to the SCI formula directly — better CPU utilization from non-blocking calls reduces the Energy term — and points at language-specific tooling like C#'s Task Parallel Library, suggesting queues, topics, or streams as a further step up from simple async calls where that fits the architecture.

Name: Use compiled languages
Guideline: Interpreted languages re-parse and compile code on every execution, consuming more energy than pre-compiled binaries, which perform compilation once and run more efficiently.
Context: The pattern names concrete language choices — Go, Rust, Java — but is careful to note compilation isn't always an option (in-browser code being the obvious exception), and recommends benchmarking your specific use case rather than assuming compiled is automatically the better fit, since compilation time itself is its own overhead to weigh.

Name: Use right-sized and energy-efficient AI models
Guideline: Select and optimize AI models that are appropriately sized for the task to reduce compute, memory, and energy consumption during training and inference.
Context: The pattern's concrete techniques are quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation for shrinking a model after the fact, with Hugging Face Optimum named as a tool for applying them and ML CO2 Impact named specifically for estimating the carbon emissions of training and inference before and after.

Name: Use server-side rendering for high-traffic pages
Guideline: Server-side rendering pre-renders templates on the server rather than the client, reducing client-side energy consumption, improving load times and network round-trips, and enabling caching benefits for high-traffic sites.
Context: The pattern points at existing framework support — Angular and React both have established server-side rendering implementations — and adds that caching the pre-rendered output specifically for frequently-accessed pages is what compounds the server-load savings on top of the client-side energy reduction.

Name: Delete unused storage resources
Guideline: From an embodied carbon perspective, it is better to delete unused storage resources so that hardware use is efficient and the storage layer is optimised for the task.
Context: The pattern's explicit caution: weigh the risk of losing something you'll actually need later against the cost and embodied-carbon savings of deleting it — this pattern is about genuinely unused storage, not an argument for aggressive deletion of anything merely idle.

Name: Match utilization requirements of virtual machines (VMs)
Guideline: It is better to have one VM running at a higher utilization than two running at low utilization rates, both in terms of energy proportionality and embodied carbon.
Context: The pattern's concrete mechanism is adjusting the actual resource allocation — adding vCPUs for high CPU usage, trimming memory that's going unused — and it works best paired with auto-scaling so the right-sized baseline can still absorb genuine traffic spikes without under-provisioning.

Name: Match utilization requirements with pre-configured servers
Guideline: It is better to have fewer, better-utilised pre-configured servers than many under-utilised ones, both in terms of energy proportionality and embodied carbon.
Context: The pattern recommends pairing this consolidation with auto-scaling specifically, so the now-fewer, better-utilized servers can still absorb traffic spikes — with lower cloud infrastructure cost typically following as a side effect of the efficiency gain.

Name: Optimise storage utilization
Guideline: It is better to maximise storage utilisation so the storage layer is optimised for the task, both in terms of energy proportionality and embodied carbon.
Context: The pattern's mechanism is literally moving data off underutilized storage volumes to consolidate onto fewer, more heavily-used ones — and it specifically cautions organizations without auto-scaling capability to balance this consolidation against the need to still handle workload spikes.

Name: Optimize average CPU utilization
Guideline: CPU usage and utilization varies throughout the day, sometimes wildly, for different computational requirements, so optimizing average CPU utilization improves overall efficiency.
Context: The pattern deliberately avoids giving a fixed target number, since the right average depends on your system: one that scales quickly can safely run a higher average utilization, while a slower-scaling system needs more headroom (a lower average) to absorb spikes without falling over.

Name: Optimize peak CPU utilization
Guideline: CPU usage and utilization varies throughout the day, sometimes wildly, for different computational requirements, so optimizing peak CPU utilization reduces the need for over-provisioned capacity.
Context: The pattern's point is to fix peaks at the software level rather than throwing more hardware at them: caching layers, reducing the data transmitted and rendered, and queuing non-urgent requests are all named as ways to smooth a peak instead of provisioning permanent capacity to absorb it.

Name: Optimize power consumption for edge AI inference
Guideline: Address power optimization on resource-constrained edge devices running AI inference through scheduling and thermal management techniques.
Context: The pattern's concrete design: three operational modes — Performance, Balanced, Power Saver — that adjust frequency, model complexity, and workload deferral based on battery and thermal state, calibrated using a feedback loop that tracks energy-per-inference, latency, and accuracy together rather than optimizing any one in isolation.

Name: Remove unused assets
Guideline: Unused cloud resources such as databases, storage buckets, and compute instances continue to consume energy and generate embodied carbon, so they should be identified and removed.
Context: The pattern's concrete monitoring approach: watch both application usage data and the cloud bill itself as signals for what's unused, and its example of consolidation is combining several underutilized database instances into fewer, more heavily-used ones rather than just deleting things outright.

Name: Scale down applications when not in use
Guideline: Applications consume CPU even when they are not actively in use, for example through background timers, garbage collection, and health checks, so idle applications should be scaled down.
Context: The pattern points at built-in tooling most cloud providers and Kubernetes already offer for scheduled scale-down, and suggests serverless architecture as an alternative path to the same outcome — not needing a schedule at all, since idle time simply doesn't get billed or run.

Name: Scale down kubernetes applications when not in use
Guideline: Dev and test Kubernetes clusters can turn off nodes outside of office hours to avoid consuming energy when workloads are not in use.
Context: The pattern's mechanism requires no code changes: pods get scaled to zero replicas on a schedule, selected via Kubernetes Labels or Annotations — it's explicitly framed as suited to Dev/Test clusters with predictable off-hours, not production environments that need to stay available.

Name: Scale infrastructure with user load
Guideline: Most applications run without taking resource demand into consideration, resulting in underused and inefficient resources; scaling infrastructure with actual user load avoids this waste.
Context: The pattern's suggested starting point: inspect CPU load data to identify specifically which VMs are underutilized, then start with the simplest available optimization (consolidating or scheduling shutdowns) before moving to more complex scaling automation.

Name: Scale Kubernetes workloads based on relevant demand metrics
Guideline: Scaling workloads based on relevant demand metrics that drive application scaling, such as HTTP requests, queue length, and cloud alerting events, can help reduce resource utilization.
Context: The pattern's concrete tool is KEDA, which enables event-driven Kubernetes scaling down to zero replicas when there's no demand — for workloads with predictable patterns instead of variable demand, it notes time-based scaling is a simpler alternative to building demand-metric-driven autoscaling.

Name: Set storage retention policies
Guideline: From an embodied carbon perspective, it is better to have an automated mechanism to delete unused storage resources so that hardware use remains efficient.
Context: The pattern ties this specifically to the embodied-carbon (M) term of the SCI equation rather than the energy term, and notes automating retention this way also cuts the ongoing operational overhead of someone having to remember to delete things manually.

Name: Time-shift Kubernetes cron jobs
Guideline: Carbon-aware time scheduling involves scheduling workloads, such as Kubernetes cron jobs, to execute when electricity carbon intensity is low.
Context: The pattern's concrete data source is 24-hour carbon-intensity forecasts from providers like Electricity Maps, and it's explicit this works at the platform level with no application code changes needed — though jobs with tight scheduling constraints or dependencies on other jobs are harder to reschedule this way.

Name: Use carbon-aware scheduling and region selection for AI workloads
Guideline: Reduce the carbon impact of AI workloads by running them in lower-carbon-intensity grid regions or during periods of high renewable energy availability.
Context: The pattern names concrete tooling for this: the Carbon Aware SDK, WattTime, and cloud-provider dashboards like Google Cloud's Sustainability Regions, AWS's Customer Carbon Footprint Tool, or Azure's Emissions Impact Dashboard — the guidance is to weigh carbon intensity as one factor alongside cost, latency, and availability when picking a region, not as an override of the others.

Name: Use circuit breaker patterns
Guideline: If a dependent application is not reachable, all network requests against it will fail and future network requests are futile; a circuit breaker avoids wasting resources on these futile calls.
Context: The pattern adds two implementation specifics: an automatic back-off strategy that re-enables requests once the failing dependency recovers, and treating a brief outage differently from a prolonged one, rather than applying the same circuit-breaker response regardless of how long the dependency has actually been down.

Name: Scan for vulnerabilities
Guideline: Implement vulnerability scanning and endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools to minimize the window of opportunity for attackers and mitigate potential malicious usage of resources, reducing the unnecessary embodied carbon emissions from compromised infrastructure.
Context: The pattern's specific recommendation: use cloud-native EDR and vulnerability-scanning services that scale with demand, rather than always-on dedicated security infrastructure — so the security tooling meant to prevent wasted resources doesn't end up being a disproportionate resource cost itself.

Name: Use cloud native network security tools and controls
Guideline: Implement network and web application firewalls to block unauthorized transmissions and filter traffic at the source, using cloud-native security tools that scale dynamically with demand to reduce unnecessary data transmission and energy consumption.
Context: The pattern frames this within a zero-trust model specifically — layered security controls rather than a single perimeter — and stresses automating the deployment and configuration of these tools themselves, so the security layer scales and updates without manual per-change effort.

Name: Use DDoS protection
Guideline: Implement DDoS protection services from cloud providers to mitigate distributed denial-of-service attacks that waste environmental resources through excessive, meaningless requests.
Context: The pattern names concrete services — AWS Shield, Azure DDoS Protection, GCP DDoS Protection, CloudFlare — and frames the sustainability angle specifically: blocking the attack traffic reduces the functional-unit term (R) in the SCI equation, since fewer requests are actually being served regardless of how efficiently each one runs.

Name: Encrypt what is necessary
Guideline: Data protection through encryption is a crucial aspect of security measures; however, the encryption process can be resource-intensive at multiple levels, so only encrypt what is actually necessary.
Context: The pattern's concrete practice: physically segregate sensitive from non-sensitive data into separate storage so only the sensitive portion needs encrypting, and choose the encryption algorithm and hashing iteration count based on your actual performance/security needs — it flags this is much harder to retrofit than to design in from the start.

Name: Match your service level objectives to business needs
Guideline: If service downtime is acceptable, it is better not to strive for the highest availability but to design the solution according to real business needs; lower availability guarantees can help reduce energy consumption by using fewer infrastructure components.
Context: The pattern's concrete practice: validate the actual business reason behind a specific availability target before designing infrastructure around it, since unnecessarily high SLOs typically mean standby systems and redundancy sitting idle most of the time — accepting this means a small, deliberate tradeoff against always-on end-user experience.

Name: Shed lower priority traffic
Guideline: When resources are constrained during high-traffic events or when carbon intensity is high, more carbon emissions are generated; shedding lower-priority traffic avoids adding resources that introduce more embodied carbon and electricity demand.
Context: The pattern's concrete mechanism is an exponential shedding policy — the rate of traffic being shed increases exponentially as overall traffic climbs, rather than a flat cutoff — so the system degrades gracefully under increasing load instead of failing abruptly at one fixed threshold.
